content.title: About
content.content: Apple salad with dressing is a mix of fresh apples, leafy greens, nuts and a light dressing made from olive oil, lemon juice and honey. The apples add sweetness and crunch, while the dressing ties the flavors together for a refreshing, nutritious dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Apples are one of the most widely consumed fruits worldwide, grown in over 90 countries.
The combination of apples and nuts is a classic culinary pairing that balances sweet and nutty flavors.
Lemon juice in the dressing prevents the apples from browning, keeping them bright.
Honey not only sweetens the dressing but also provides antibacterial properties.
Apple salad is often served in the autumn season when apples are at their peak harvest.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Apples provide vitamin C, which supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: The fiber in apples aids digestion and helps maintain a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Healthy monounsaturated fats
items.content: Olive oil in the dressing contains monounsaturated fats beneficial for heart health.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids from apples and honey have antioxidant effects that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports blood sugar balance
items.content: Fiber and moderate honey content help slow the rise of blood glucose after eating.

items.title: Nut allergy
items.content: If nuts are included in the dressing, they may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Honey and apples add natural sugars, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Non‑organic apples may carry pesticide residues; using organic apples or washing thoroughly is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled, drizzling the dressing just before serving. Optional additions include walnuts, raisins, or pumpkin seeds for extra texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Store the dressing separately to prevent the greens from becoming soggy.

content.title: About
content.content: Sweet potato bread is a whole‑grain loaf that incorporates sweet potato puree into the dough. The sweet potato gives the bread a gentle orange‑brown hue, a subtle sweetness, and extra moisture. It is popular in diet‑focused nutrition because of the sweet potato’s low glycemic index and high fiber content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sweet potatoes contain more beta‑carotene than regular potatoes, giving the bread a bright color and antioxidant benefits.
Combining whole grains with sweet potato boosts B‑vitamin and mineral levels, such as potassium and magnesium.
Sweet potato bread has traditional roots in the southern United States and the Caribbean.
Sweet potato provides resistant starch, which acts as a prebiotic supporting gut health.
During baking, sweet potato helps retain moisture, resulting in a softer crust and longer shelf life.

items.title: Rich in beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene converts to vitamin A in the body, supporting vision and immune function.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Sweet potato raises blood glucose slowly, which is beneficial for blood‑sugar management.

items.title: Source of potassium and magnesium
items.content: These minerals support heart, muscle, and nervous system health.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Antioxidants protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Wheat/gluten allergy
items.content: Like any bread, it can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten intolerance.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweet potatoes are naturally sweet, so those strictly limiting sugar should account for total carbohydrate intake.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Despite its benefits, sweet potato bread remains calorie‑dense; portion control is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sweet potato bread works well toasted, as a base for sandwiches, alongside soups, or cut into croutons. Top with avocado, cottage cheese, or a light spread for a nutritious snack.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the bread in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, refrigerate or freeze sliced pieces.

content.title: About
content.content: Mackerel is a marine fish from the Scombridae family, found in temperate and subtropical seas. It has firm, slightly oily flesh with a distinctive aroma, and is rich in omega‑3 fatty acids, B‑vitamins, and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mackerel can migrate long distances, sometimes covering over 3,000 km.
In Japan, mackerel (sai) is a delicacy often served as sushi or grilled.
Mackerel grows quickly, reaching 5–6 kg within a year.
In the wild, mackerel forms large schools, making it a key target for commercial fisheries.
The flesh has a bright orange hue due to high carotenoid content.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3
items.content: Omega‑3 fatty acids support heart health, reduce inflammation, and aid brain function.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Mackerel provides complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamin B12, B6, and niacin help metabolism, nervous system function, and energy production.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Mackerel supplies selenium, iodine, and phosphorus, important for thyroid health and bones.

items.title: Eye health support
items.content: Carotenoids and vitamin A contribute to maintaining good vision.

items.title: Mercury content
items.content: Like many larger predatory fish, mackerel may contain trace amounts of mercury; pregnant women and children should limit intake.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Possible parasites
items.content: Raw or undercooked mackerel can harbor parasites; it should be cooked thoroughly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mackerel is suitable for baking, pan‑frying, grilling, smoking, and raw preparations like sushi. Before cooking, remove the scales, gut the fish, and rinse. Serve with lemon, herbs, or a teriyaki glaze.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh mackerel in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C, wrapped in plastic or in an airtight container, for up to 2 days. Frozen mackerel can be stored at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Thaw frozen fish in the fridge before use.

content.title: About
content.content: The chocolate ice cream sandwich is a dessert consisting of two soft cookies with a layer of creamy ice cream in between, coated in a chocolate glaze. It is popular in the US and Europe as a summer snack and is often sold in packs of 2–4 pieces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first ice cream sandwich appeared in the 1970s in the United States as a quick way to combine cookies and ice cream.
The chocolate version became the best‑selling thanks to the sweet chocolate and cold ice cream combination.
In some countries the sandwich is offered with extra fillings such as nuts, caramel or fruit sauces.
A single sandwich typically contains about 150–200 kcal.
Vegan versions use plant‑based milk and chocolate alternatives.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: The dairy component of the ice cream provides calcium, which is important for bones and teeth.

items.title: Contains vitamin D
items.content: Vitamin D present in dairy helps the body absorb calcium.

items.title: Quick energy boost
items.content: Sugar and fats in the chocolate coating supply rapid energy, useful on hot days.

items.title: Mood improvement
items.content: Sweet desserts stimulate serotonin production, enhancing mood.

items.title: Antioxidant content
items.content: Dark chocolate contains flavonoids that have antioxidant properties.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of cavities.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: The ice cream contains lactose, which may cause discomfort for those who are intolerant.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to casein.

items.title: Trans fat presence
items.content: Certain chocolate glazes may contain trans fats, which are harmful to heart health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sandwiches are usually eaten frozen, straight from the package. They can be paired with berries, nuts, or drizzled with extra chocolate sauce. For children, cut into small pieces to prevent choking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the freezer at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. After opening, consume within 1–2 weeks to avoid ice crystal formation.

content.title: About
content.content: Kakadu plum (Terminalia ferdinandiana) is a small, pale green to yellowish fruit native to the tropical woodlands of northern Australia. It has a single large seed, thin flesh, and a tart, slightly bitter flavor. Indigenous Australians have eaten it for thousands of years, and it is also known as gubinge or billygoat plum. It is best known as one of the richest natural sources of vitamin C.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Kakadu plum has one of the highest recorded vitamin C contents of any fruit, many times higher than oranges by weight.
It grows wild in northern Australia, including the Kakadu region of the Northern Territory and the Kimberley.
Indigenous Australians have used the fruit as food and medicine for thousands of years.
The fruit is small, about the size of an olive, with a large seed and little flesh.
It is most commonly sold as a powder, puree, or in jams, sauces, and skin care products.

items.title: Extremely rich in vitamin C
items.content: Kakadu plum is an outstanding source of vitamin C, which supports the immune system and skin.

items.title: Contains polyphenols
items.content: It contains plant compounds such as ellagic acid and gallic acid with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Provides vitamin E
items.content: Kakadu plum contains some vitamin E, an antioxidant.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: The fruit contributes some fiber.

items.title: Easy to add as a powder
items.content: Kakadu plum powder can be mixed into smoothies, yogurt, and drinks.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The fruit and powder are tart and acidic and may bother sensitive stomachs or tooth enamel.

items.title: Too much vitamin C
items.content: Very high intakes of vitamin C may cause stomach upset or diarrhea and may contribute to kidney stones in susceptible people.

items.title: Concentrated powders
items.content: Concentrated powders can supply a very large amount of vitamin C in a small serving. Follow the label.

items.title: Possible medication interactions and allergies
items.content: Vitamin C can affect some medications and lab tests, and allergies are possible. People with health conditions or taking medication should consult a healthcare professional.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fresh Kakadu plums are rarely available outside Australia. The powder can be stirred into smoothies, yogurt, oatmeal, juices, or water, and the fruit is used in jams, chutneys, sauces, and desserts. Use small amounts according to the product label.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store Kakadu plum powder in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Keep frozen fruit or puree frozen. Keep products away from moisture and light and use them by the date on the package.

pasta-with-sauce-meatless-school-lunch.title: Pasta with sauce, meatless, school lunch

content.title: About
content.content: Meat‑less pasta with sauce is a ready‑to‑serve school lunch. The pasta, made from durum wheat, is tossed in a tomato‑based sauce enriched with vegetable purées and contains no meat. The dish provides a balanced mix of carbohydrates, vitamins and minerals suitable for school‑age children.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Durum wheat pasta contains more protein and fiber than regular pasta.
Meat‑less tomato sauce is often fortified with vitamin C and lycopene, which improve iron absorption from plant sources.
The product complies with national school nutrition standards, including limits on salt and fat.
Unopened packages can be stored at room temperature for up to 12 months.
Small pieces of carrot, zucchini and sweet pepper are often added to boost nutritional value.

items.title: Energy supply
items.content: Carbohydrates from the pasta provide sustained energy and help children stay full throughout the school day.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Durum wheat is a good source of B1, B2 and niacin, which support metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Lycopene and vitamin C
items.content: The tomato sauce offers antioxidant protection, supporting immunity and protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Vegetable additions increase fiber content, promoting healthy digestion.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: The absence of meat and limited added oils make the dish suitable for reducing cardiovascular risk.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: Durum wheat pasta contains gluten, which can trigger reactions in individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: Salt is limited to meet school guidelines, but consumers should still check the label for exact amounts.

items.title: Heat treatment
items.content: The meal should be heated to at least 75 °C to ensure any potential bacteria are destroyed.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the portion in a microwave or steam oven until piping hot, then stir to distribute the sauce evenly. Optionally sprinkle a small amount of grated cheese or fresh herbs before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated at +4 °C and consume within 3‑4 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Peach strudel is a pastry made from flaky layered dough filled with fresh or canned peaches, sugar, and sometimes nuts. The dough is light and crisp, while the filling is sweet and aromatic, typical of traditional Austrian desserts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Strudel originated in Austria and first appeared in the 17th century.
Peaches used in the filling are often grown in warm climates such as Italy and Spain.
Traditional recipes include raisins, nuts, and cinnamon, but modern versions often stick to pure peach filling.
The layered dough is created by folding butter between many thin sheets of dough, giving the characteristic “layered” effect.
In some countries the strudel is served with vanilla sauce or whipped cream.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Peaches provide vitamin C, which supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber in peaches promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium contributes to normal heart function and blood pressure regulation.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Peaches contain beta‑carotene and other antioxidants that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many desserts, peach strudel contains relatively little fat when a modest amount of butter is used in the dough.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: The filling is often sweetened, so people monitoring blood sugar should watch portion size.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The dough contains wheat flour, making the strudel unsuitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Layered pastry is calorie‑dense, so moderation is recommended.

items.title: Possible preservatives
items.content: Canned peaches may contain additives; using fresh fruit is preferable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve peach strudel warm, lightly dusted with powdered sugar. It can be enjoyed on its own or paired with vanilla ice cream, whipped cream, or a berry sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the finished strudel in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days or in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze it wrapped in plastic film and aluminum foil.

stuffed-pepper-with-rice-and-meat.title: Stuffed Pepper with Rice and Meat

content.title: About
content.content: Stuffed pepper with rice and meat is a classic dish of Slavic cuisine. Sweet or hot bell peppers are filled with a mixture of boiled rice, ground meat (usually beef or pork), onion, carrot and spices, then baked until tender. The dish combines aromatic meat, fluffy rice and the mild sweetness of the pepper.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Stuffed pepper appeared in Russia in the 19th century as a local adaptation of the Turkish dolma.
Traditional recipes often add tomato paste or sauce to the filling for extra juiciness.
Peppers are sometimes blanched before stuffing to make them easier to open.
Different Russian regions use different meats: Siberia often adds venison, the Volga region prefers pork.
The dish is commonly served with sour cream or a tomato‑based sauce.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: The meat in the filling provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Rice supplies slowly digestible carbs, helping maintain steady energy levels.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Peppers are high in vitamin C, while the meat and rice contribute iron, zinc and B‑vitamins.

items.title: Low added sugar
items.content: The dish contains no added sugars, making it suitable for moderate‑sugar diets.

items.title: Fiber content
items.content: Both pepper and rice add dietary fiber, supporting healthy digestion.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to bell peppers, gluten (if a sauce is used) or certain meats.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Prepared sauces or salty seasonings can raise the sodium content of the dish.

items.title: Thorough cooking required
items.content: Meat must be fully cooked to avoid food‑borne illness.

items.title: Dietary restrictions
items.content: People on gluten‑free diets should check sauce ingredients and use gluten‑free spices.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the stuffed pepper hot, often alongside mashed potatoes, a fresh salad or a dollop of sour cream. It can be eaten straight from the baking dish or the filling can be lifted with a fork. Leftovers store well in the refrigerator and reheat in the oven or microwave.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the dish to room temperature, then place it in an airtight container and refrigerate for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Trail mix is a blend of dried fruits, nuts, seeds, and sometimes chocolate pieces, designed to provide quick energy during long hikes, running workouts, and other active pursuits. The NFS (No Fruit Sugar) version contains only the natural sugars from dried fruit without any added sugar.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Trail mix originated in the United States in the early 20th century as a convenient snack for hikers and athletes.
Formulations vary widely, from classic nut‑and‑raisin combos to exotic mixes with cranberry, mango, and pumpkin seeds.
The NFS version is popular among people monitoring glycemic response because dried fruits provide only inherent sugars.
Nuts in the mix are a good source of plant protein and healthy fats.
Trail mix is often packaged in small, single‑serve bags, making it easy to carry in a backpack.

items.title: Rapid energy replenishment
items.content: Dried fruits supply quick‑acting carbohydrates, while nuts provide a slower release of energy through fats and protein.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Nuts are rich in mono‑ and polyunsaturated fatty acids that promote heart health.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Both dried fruits and seeds boost fiber content, aiding digestion.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: The mix contains vitamin E, magnesium, iron, and potassium, important for muscle function and electrolyte balance.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Fruits like cranberry and blueberry add polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Tree‑nut allergy
items.content: Trail mix often includes peanuts, almonds, cashews, and other nuts that can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: The combination of nuts and dried fruit makes the product energy‑dense; portion control is advisable, especially on calorie‑restricted diets.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some mixes are salted; individuals watching sodium intake should choose unsalted versions.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Even without added sugar, dried fruits contain natural sugars that can affect blood glucose levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Trail mix is convenient to eat straight from the bag during a hike, run, or bike ride. It can be tossed into yogurt, oatmeal, or smoothies for extra nutrition. For a richer flavor, lightly toast the mix in a dry skillet before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store trail mix in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. For longer shelf life, keep it in the refrigerator to prevent the nuts from going rancid. Discard any portion that smells off or shows discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Vodka and lemonade is a popular cocktail that blends the neutral taste of vodka with the refreshing sweetness of lemonade. It is often served in tall glasses over ice with a lemon wedge.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The drink originated in the United States in the 1970s as a simple summer beverage.
There are many variations: flavored vodkas, added mint, or fruit syrups can be used.
Traditional lemonade is made from fresh lemon juice, sugar and water, without carbonation.
Vodka and lemonade is a common choice at barbecues and picnics because it can be prepared in large batches.

items.title: Moderate consumption may promote relaxation
items.content: Small amounts of alcohol have a calming effect, helping to reduce stress.

items.title: Vitamin C from lemonade
items.content: Fresh lemon juice provides vitamin C, which supports the immune system.

items.title: Alcohol intoxication
items.content: Excessive vodka intake leads to alcohol poisoning and long‑term health issues.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Prepared lemonade often contains a high amount of sugar, which can raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Interaction with medications
items.content: Alcohol can amplify the effects of certain drugs; consult a physician if you take medication.

content.title: How to Make
content.content: Combine 50 ml vodka with 150 ml freshly made lemonade, add ice and a lemon wedge. Optionally garnish with a sprig of mint.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store vodka in a tightly sealed bottle in a cool, dark place. Lemonade is best made just before serving, but it can be kept in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours.
